title: Ezekiel 41:1–14
context: The guide brings the prophet into the house itself. He measures the nave, forty cubits long and twenty wide, and then goes inward alone to measure the inner room, twenty cubits square, and says, “This is the most holy place.” He measures the thick wall of the house and the side rooms built around it in three stories, thirty in each, wider at the higher levels. He then measures the raised base, the open area around the house, a large building on the west, and the overall dimensions of the temple area, one hundred cubits each way. Several measures echo Solomon's temple, including the width of twenty cubits (1 Kings 6:2) and the inner sanctuary of twenty cubits (1 Kings 6:20).

verses.text: He brought me to the nave and measured the posts, six cubits wide on the one side and six cubits wide on the other side, which was the width of the tent.
verses.arminianNotes: “He brought me to the nave and measured the posts.” Arminian readers see the guide entering the main hall of the house, with its posts six cubits wide on each side.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the phrase “the width of the tent,” which may recall the tabernacle. The vision links the new house with Israel's earlier places of worship.

verses.text: The width of the entrance was ten cubits, and the sides of the entrance were five cubits on the one side, and five cubits on the other side. He measured its length, forty cubits, and the width, twenty cubits.
verses.arminianNotes: “The width of the entrance was ten cubits.” Arminian readers see the nave measured at “forty cubits” long and “twenty cubits” wide, a large hall before the inner room.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the width of twenty cubits matches Solomon's temple, whose width was “twenty” in 1 Kings 6:2. The new house stands in continuity with the old.

verses.text: Then he went inward and measured each post of the entrance, two cubits; and the entrance, six cubits; and the width of the entrance, seven cubits.
verses.arminianNotes: “Then he went inward and measured each post of the entrance.” Arminian readers see the guide alone going inward to the innermost room, while the prophet's narration follows.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the prophet, a priest, does not say he entered the most holy place. Many see in this restraint a reflection of the holiness of that room.

verses.text: He measured its length, twenty cubits, and the width, twenty cubits, before the nave. He said to me, “This is the most holy place.”
verses.arminianNotes: He said to me, “This is the most holy place.” Arminian readers see the guide naming the inner room, twenty cubits long and twenty wide, as the holiest part of the house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Solomon's inner sanctuary was also “twenty cubits in length, and twenty cubits in width” (1 Kings 6:20). Hebrews 9:3 speaks of the “Holy of Holies” in the tabernacle.

verses.text: Then he measured the wall of the house, six cubits; and the width of every side room, four cubits, all around the house on every side.
verses.arminianNotes: “Then he measured the wall of the house, six cubits.” Arminian readers see a thick wall around the house and side rooms four cubits wide around every side.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Solomon's temple also had side rooms around it (1 Kings 6:5). The vision again recalls the earlier temple's design while giving its own measures.

verses.text: The side rooms were in three stories, one over another, and thirty in each story. They entered into the wall which belonged to the house for the side rooms all around, that they might be supported and not penetrate the wall of the house.
verses.arminianNotes: “The side rooms were in three stories, one over another, and thirty in each story.” Arminian readers see rooms built so that they rested on the wall without cutting into it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the rooms were supported so as “not penetrate the wall of the house.” Many see in this care a respect for the integrity of the sanctuary itself.

verses.text: The side rooms were wider on the higher levels, because the walls were narrower at the higher levels. Therefore the width of the house increased upward; and so one went up from the lowest level to the highest through the middle level.
verses.arminianNotes: “The side rooms were wider on the higher levels.” Arminian readers see that because the walls narrowed as they rose, the rooms grew wider, with access from the lowest to the highest level through the middle.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the precise building details suggest a real structure in the prophet's vision. Literal and symbolic readers both take such details as meaningful parts of the whole.

verses.text: I saw also that the house had a raised base all around. The foundations of the side rooms were a full reed of six great cubits.
verses.arminianNotes: “I saw also that the house had a raised base all around.” Arminian readers see the house set on a platform, with foundations measured as “a full reed of six great cubits.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the raised base sets the house above its surroundings. The theme of elevation runs through the vision, from the high mountain to the steps of the courts.

verses.text: The thickness of the outer wall of the side rooms was five cubits. That which was left was the place of the side rooms that belonged to the house.
verses.arminianNotes: “The thickness of the outer wall of the side rooms was five cubits.” Arminian readers see the outer wall of the side rooms measured and the remaining space belonging to the house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that every part of the house is accounted for. The vision presents a complete and well-defined sanctuary, with nothing left undefined.

verses.text: Between the rooms was a width of twenty cubits around the house on every side.
verses.arminianNotes: “Between the rooms was a width of twenty cubits around the house on every side.” Arminian readers see open space between the house and other rooms, setting the house apart.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the open space separates the house from surrounding buildings. Many see in such separation a picture of holiness, as 42:20 later states.

verses.text: The doors of the side rooms were toward an open area that was left, one door toward the north, and another door toward the south. The width of the open area was five cubits all around.
verses.arminianNotes: “The doors of the side rooms were toward an open area that was left.” Arminian readers see the side rooms entered from the north and the south, with an open area five cubits wide.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the care given to access and space. The arrangement keeps the house itself distinct, while providing for the work carried on around it.

verses.text: The building that was before the separate place at the side toward the west was seventy cubits wide; and the wall of the building was five cubits thick all around, and its length ninety cubits.
verses.arminianNotes: “The building that was before the separate place at the side toward the west was seventy cubits wide.” Arminian readers see a large building on the west whose purpose the text does not explain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the building's use is not stated, and readers have offered different suggestions. Both traditions leave the question open rather than supplying a purpose the text does not give.

verses.text: So he measured the temple, one hundred cubits long; and the separate place, and the building, with its walls, one hundred cubits long;
verses.arminianNotes: “So he measured the temple, one hundred cubits long.” Arminian readers see the overall length of the temple and the area behind it, each measured at one hundred cubits.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the round measure of one hundred again expresses completeness. The house fits within a carefully proportioned plan.

verses.text: also the width of the face of the temple, and of the separate place toward the east, one hundred cubits.
verses.arminianNotes: “also the width of the face of the temple, and of the separate place toward the east, one hundred cubits.” Arminian readers see the front of the temple area measured to the same width.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the equal length and width form a square, like the inner court in 40:47. The repeated squares give the whole complex a sense of balance and wholeness.
